primary_claim: Small instruction-tuned language models (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-1B-Instruct) have specialized attention heads that detect epistemic uncertainty on fictional/out-of-distribution questions, but this detected uncertainty is subsequently suppressed by other heads downstream in the circuit, producing a confident hallucinated answer instead of an admission of uncertainty.

effect.metric: change in uncertainty mass (probability on uncertainty-expressing tokens) from head ablation / activation patching
effect.value: Activation patching of head L11H3 reduced uncertainty mass by ~14% in Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and by 7% (L8H11) in Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct; ablating detected 'uncertainty-suppressor' heads increased uncertainty mass (delta-delta up to +8.06e-05), while ablating 'uncertainty-detector' heads decreased it (delta-delta down to -4.41e-05)

stated_future_work: Extend the research to cover Reasoning and MoE LLMs, not just small dense models
Expand the dataset to include logical fallacies and math inconsistencies, not just fictional-entity prompts
Create a mechanism to control this uncertainty circuit and test the resulting model on a hallucination benchmark
Investigate whether larger models learn not to suppress uncertainty due to stronger RLHF, potentially helping reduce RLHF/post-training cost
limitations_stated: Research doesn't cover Reasoning or MoE LLMs
Dataset is limited to fictional-entity prompts and lacks diversity such as logical fallacies or math inconsistencies
The full uncertainty circuit has not been discovered, since ablating/patching a single head (L11H3) only reduces uncertainty mass by about 14%, implying more heads are involved
Experiments cover only 1B-parameter models, so it cannot be concluded why larger models tend to admit uncertainty instead of hallucinating
quote: So Small Language Models do detect epistemic uncertainty as key heads detect OOD tokens which is later suppressed in downstream layer.
